column1: Define reusable server-side logic with {{c1::CREATE PROCEDURE}} dbo.GetCustomerOrders AS BEGIN SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders; END;
column2:
The statement stores the named operation. Use EXEC in a separate call to run the SELECT later.
Review source

column1: Introduce a procedure's body with CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetCustomerOrders {{c1::AS}} SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders;
column2:
AS separates the procedure header from its implementation. Here the body reads order identifiers.
Review source

column1: In an ordinary T-SQL procedure, {{c1::BEGIN and END}} group body statements but do not start a transaction.
column2:
The block controls which statements are grouped together. It does not make several writes commit or roll back as a unit without transaction control.
Review source

column1: Call an existing procedure with {{c1::EXEC}} dbo.GetCustomerOrders;
column2:
EXEC asks SQL Server to run the existing object. Use the schema-qualified name to identify the intended procedure.
Review source

column1: Declare an integer procedure parameter named CustomerID as {{c1::@CustomerID INT}}.
column2:
Start the parameter name with @ and follow it with the type. This declaration accepts an integer value supplied by the caller.
Review source

column1: Make a start-date parameter optional with @StartDate DATETIME {{c1::= NULL}}.
column2:
SQL Server supplies NULL if the caller omits the argument. The procedure body still decides how to handle a missing start date.
Review source

column1: Declare a calculated output value with @TotalAmount DECIMAL(10,2) {{c1::OUTPUT}}.
column2:
The marker allows the caller to receive the value assigned within the procedure. The call must also use OUTPUT with a receiving variable.
Review source

column1: Receive an output value with DECLARE @Total DECIMAL(10,2); EXEC dbo.CalculateOrderTotal @OrderID = 1, @TotalAmount = @Total {{c1::OUTPUT}};
column2:
The procedure assigns its parameter value back to @Total because the call marks it OUTPUT. Without that marker, the local variable is not updated.
Review source

column1: Capture a procedure's return code with DECLARE @Status INT; EXEC {{c1::@Status =}} dbo.GetCustomerOrders;
column2:
The assignment before the procedure name captures the integer status. A result set produced by SELECT is sent separately.
Review source

column1: An ordinary T-SQL procedure is normally compiled {{c1::when it first executes}}, not when CREATE PROCEDURE stores its definition.
column2:
Creating the procedure stores its definition. For ordinary procedures, the engine normally compiles statements on first use and can reuse eligible plans later.
Review source

column1: Suppress affected-row count messages with {{c1::SET NOCOUNT ON}}; inside a procedure.
column2:
This setting suppresses separate count messages, not query data. A SELECT inside the procedure still returns its result set.
Review source

column1: Read {{c1::@@ROWCOUNT}} immediately after the statement whose affected-row count you need, even when NOCOUNT is ON.
column2:
Read @@ROWCOUNT immediately after the statement whose count you need because later statements can overwrite it. NOCOUNT does not disable that count.
Review source

column1: WHERE (@StartDate {{c1::IS NULL}} OR OrderDate >= @StartDate) treats NULL as no lower date bound.
column2:
When @StartDate is NULL, the first condition allows rows through without a lower date limit. Otherwise the date comparison supplies that limit.
Review source

column1: Inside CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_MESSAGE()}} returns the caught error's message text.
column2:
This function gives the message text of the error handled by the current CATCH. It does not return the error number or severity.
Review source

column1: Inside CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_SEVERITY()}} returns the caught error's severity level.
column2:
Severity describes the level of the error caught by this block. It is separate from the error's number and state.
Review source

column1: Inside CATCH, {{c1::ERROR_STATE()}} returns the caught error's state number.
column2:
The state helps distinguish where an error was raised when several places use the same error number. Read it in CATCH with the other error details.
Review source

column1: For a procedure that owns its transaction, guard cleanup with IF {{c1::@@TRANCOUNT > 0}} ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
column2:
The guard avoids issuing ROLLBACK with no open transaction. Use it here only because the procedure owns the transaction it is rolling back.
Review source

column1: Raise an input-validation error with {{c1::THROW}} 50001, 'CustomerID must be a positive integer.', 1;
column2:
This form raises a new user-defined error with severity 16. The number identifies the error and the last argument supplies its state.
Review source

column1: To preserve the error caught by CATCH instead of raising a replacement, use {{c1::THROW;}} without arguments.
column2:
Without arguments, THROW rethrows the error being handled. It preserves details that would otherwise be replaced by a newly constructed error.
Review source

column1: In the legacy call RAISERROR('Invalid input.', 16, 1), 16 specifies the error's {{c1::severity}}.
column2:
The second argument describes the severity of the message. The third is a separate state value that can identify the place that raised it.
Review source

column1: A descriptive procedure name commonly starts with a {{c1::verb}}, such as Get, Update, or Calculate.
column2:
A verb tells readers what calling the procedure does. CalculateOrderTotal describes the operation without naming the tables it uses.
Review source
